questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Applying the ISC2 ethical canons when organizational interests conflict with public safety
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize duties under the professional code when competing obligations arise
questions.scenarioContext: A security manager learns that an executive intends to conceal a serious weakness in a public transportation control environment until after a pending financing announcement. The weakness could expose passengers to physical harm, and the executive orders the manager to remain silent.
questions.prompt: Which consideration should guide the security manager's response FIRST?

choices.A: Protecting the employer's financing strategy and confidential business plans
choices.B: Advancing the security profession by publishing technical details of the weakness
choices.C: Protecting society and public safety through appropriate escalation and lawful action
choices.D: Following the executive's instruction until an internal audit confirms the weakness

questions.explanation: The duty to protect society, the common good, and public trust has priority when credible physical harm is possible. Appropriate escalation and lawful reporting address that duty without unnecessarily disclosing sensitive technical details. Protecting the employer is important but does not override public safety, immediate publication could create additional risk, and waiting for an audit would leave a serious known exposure untreated.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Distinguishing due diligence from due care in an enterprise security program
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the management activity that demonstrates informed risk investigation
questions.scenarioContext: Before approving a new customer platform, a board committee requests an asset inventory, reviews applicable obligations, examines threat information, and commissions a risk assessment. Management will select and operate safeguards after reviewing the results.
questions.prompt: The committee's actions MOST directly demonstrate which concept?

choices.A: Due diligence, because decision-makers are systematically identifying and evaluating risk
choices.B: Due care, because the selected safeguards are already operating effectively
choices.C: Risk transfer, because the assessment shifts accountability to the assessors
choices.D: Non-repudiation, because the committee can prove that the review occurred

questions.explanation: Due diligence is the ongoing process of investigating, understanding, and evaluating risk before and during decision-making. Due care is demonstrated by taking reasonable protective action based on that knowledge, which occurs later in this scenario. An assessment does not transfer accountability, and a record of the review alone does not establish non-repudiation of business transactions.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Aligning security governance with business objectives
questions.performanceIndicator: Select governance metrics that connect security decisions to organizational outcomes
questions.scenarioContext: A manufacturer is expanding a time-sensitive distribution service. Executives believe the security program produces many technical reports but does not show whether it supports the expansion strategy.
questions.prompt: What should the CISO do FIRST to improve security governance?

choices.A: Increase the number of vulnerability findings reported each month
choices.B: Map security objectives and risk measures to the expansion's business goals and risk appetite
choices.C: Require every business unit to use identical technical safeguards
choices.D: Delegate acceptance of strategic security risk to the operations team

questions.explanation: Effective governance begins by aligning security objectives, priorities, and measures with business goals and approved risk appetite. More vulnerability counts may add operational data without demonstrating strategic value. Uniform safeguards can ignore differing business risks, and operational personnel should not be assigned acceptance authority for strategic risk unless governance has explicitly granted it.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Recognizing complementary foundational security properties
questions.performanceIndicator: Match business assurance needs to authenticity and non-repudiation concepts
questions.prompt: A digital approval process must establish that a message came from the claimed sender and provide strong evidence that the sender cannot credibly deny approving it. Which 2 security properties address these requirements? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Availability
choices.B: Authenticity
choices.C: Confidentiality
choices.D: Non-repudiation
choices.E: Fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Authenticity supports confidence that the message and sender are genuine, while non-repudiation provides evidence intended to prevent a party from successfully denying an action. Confidentiality limits disclosure, availability concerns timely access, and fault tolerance supports continued operation; none of those three directly satisfies both stated approval requirements.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Assigning accountability within security governance roles
questions.performanceIndicator: Differentiate business ownership of risk from advisory security responsibilities
questions.scenarioContext: A retail enterprise identifies a residual risk in an order-processing service after reasonable safeguards are applied. The security office documented the exposure, but the service owner wants the security analyst to accept the risk on behalf of the business.
questions.prompt: Who should normally make the risk acceptance decision?

choices.A: The security analyst who performed the assessment
choices.B: The external assessor who confirmed the residual risk
choices.C: The business owner with authority and accountability for the affected service
choices.D: The system administrator responsible for implementing safeguards

questions.explanation: Risk acceptance belongs to the accountable business owner or another properly authorized decision-maker who understands the business consequences. Security analysts advise and document, assessors provide independent findings, and administrators implement controls. Those roles do not normally own the business impact or possess delegated authority to accept it.

questions.competency: I.A — Professional Ethics, Core Security Concepts, and Governance Principles
questions.skill: Integrating security governance into an acquisition
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the earliest governance activity needed to understand inherited security risk
questions.scenarioContext: An organization plans to acquire a smaller firm whose systems will be connected to the parent network immediately after closing. The target has not used the parent's security control framework.
questions.prompt: Which action should security leadership recommend as the HIGHEST priority before integration?

choices.A: Perform risk-based security due diligence and define remediation or integration conditions
choices.B: Replace every target system before assessing its business importance
choices.C: Delay all security review until ownership legally transfers
choices.D: Accept the target's risks because the acquisition sponsor approved the transaction

questions.explanation: Pre-integration due diligence reveals inherited exposure, legal obligations, control gaps, and conditions that should influence the acquisition and integration plan. Wholesale replacement before assessment is not risk-based. Waiting until after transfer sacrifices the opportunity to establish conditions, while deal approval does not itself constitute informed acceptance of unidentified security risk.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Classifying legal proceedings and their standards of proof
questions.performanceIndicator: Distinguish criminal prosecution from civil and administrative matters
questions.scenarioContext: A government prosecutor alleges that an individual intentionally committed a computer offense prohibited by statute. A conviction could result in imprisonment.
questions.prompt: Which legal category and general standard of proof apply?

choices.A: Civil law and proof by clear organizational policy
choices.B: Criminal law and proof beyond a reasonable doubt
choices.C: Administrative law and proof beyond all possible doubt
choices.D: Contract law and proof by technical consensus

questions.explanation: A government prosecution for a statutory offense that can lead to imprisonment is criminal, and the prosecution generally must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Civil disputes commonly use a lower standard such as preponderance of the evidence. Administrative matters depend on the governing regime, and neither organizational policy nor technical consensus is a legal standard of proof.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Applying the policy hierarchy to mandatory configuration requirements
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose the document type that establishes compulsory and measurable requirements
questions.scenarioContext: A university's policy states that sensitive information must be protected. Security leadership now needs a mandatory organization-wide document specifying minimum authentication settings that can be tested consistently.
questions.prompt: Which type of document should contain these detailed mandatory requirements?

choices.A: Guideline
choices.B: Procedure
choices.C: Standard
choices.D: Mission statement

questions.explanation: A standard translates high-level policy into specific, mandatory, and measurable requirements. A procedure gives step-by-step instructions for performing a task, while a guideline offers recommended flexibility. A mission statement expresses broad organizational purpose and is not the appropriate vehicle for testable authentication settings.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Preserving evidence when an internal matter may become criminal
questions.performanceIndicator: Select an investigation response that preserves admissibility and coordinates authority
questions.scenarioContext: During an authorized administrative investigation, an investigator finds evidence suggesting deliberate financial fraud. Management believes law enforcement may become involved, but no referral has yet been made.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST next action?

choices.A: Continue informal interviews until the suspected employee confesses
choices.B: Immediately publish the findings to warn other employees
choices.C: Preserve evidence under documented procedures and consult legal counsel about escalation
choices.D: Delete unrelated evidence so the investigation file remains concise

questions.explanation: Potential criminal proceedings require disciplined evidence preservation, documented handling, and coordination with legal counsel so investigative authority and referral obligations are respected. Informal questioning may compromise the investigation, publication can violate confidentiality and due process, and deleting material before lawful relevance and retention decisions are made can damage evidentiary integrity.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Protecting intellectual property through appropriate legal mechanisms
questions.performanceIndicator: Differentiate trademark and trade secret protection in a business scenario
questions.prompt: An organization wants to protect both its distinctive product logo and a confidential manufacturing method that derives value from remaining secret. Which 2 forms of intellectual property protection are MOST directly applicable? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Copyright for the confidential manufacturing method
choices.B: Trademark for the distinctive product logo
choices.C: Trade secret protection for the confidential manufacturing method
choices.D: Patent protection automatically created without filing or disclosure
choices.E: Software license protection for the product logo

questions.explanation: Trademark law is designed to protect source-identifying marks such as a distinctive product logo. A valuable confidential method can qualify as a trade secret when reasonable measures preserve its secrecy. Copyright does not protect a functional method itself, patent rights are not created automatically, and a software license is not the relevant protection for a brand logo.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Assessing obligations before transborder data transfer
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the governance review required before changing international data processing
questions.scenarioContext: A global services company intends to move personal data from customers in one jurisdiction to a processing center in another. The project team argues that encryption alone makes legal review unnecessary.
questions.prompt: What should the privacy and security leaders do FIRST?

choices.A: Approve the move because encryption eliminates jurisdictional obligations
choices.B: Determine applicable transfer restrictions, lawful mechanisms, contracts, and data-location requirements
choices.C: Copy all data to the new location and assess obligations after operations stabilize
choices.D: Treat the move solely as an internal technical architecture decision

questions.explanation: Cross-border processing must be evaluated against the laws, transfer mechanisms, contractual commitments, and location restrictions that apply to the data and jurisdictions involved. Encryption can reduce risk but does not eliminate legal duties. Moving first creates avoidable exposure, and classifying the change as purely technical ignores governance and privacy requirements.

questions.competency: I.B — Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Issues, Investigations, and the Policy Hierarchy
questions.skill: Coordinating breach response with jurisdiction-specific obligations
questions.performanceIndicator: Select the initial governance action for a potentially reportable breach
questions.scenarioContext: A travel company discovers that customer records may have been accessed without authorization. Affected customers reside in several jurisdictions, and the facts are still developing.
questions.prompt: Which action is MOST appropriate at this stage?

choices.A: Wait for complete certainty before activating any breach process
choices.B: Notify every possible authority immediately using an unverified incident count
choices.C: Activate the incident and legal assessment process, preserve facts, and track applicable notification deadlines
choices.D: Let the technical team decide whether legal notification is necessary

questions.explanation: The organization should promptly activate coordinated incident, privacy, and legal assessment; preserve reliable facts; determine affected jurisdictions; and manage applicable deadlines. Waiting for perfect certainty may cause missed obligations, while premature unverified notices can be inaccurate. Notification decisions require authorized legal and business input, not an isolated technical determination.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Calculating annualized loss expectancy
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply SLE and ARO values to a quantitative risk estimate
questions.prompt: An illustrative risk analysis estimates a single loss expectancy of $80,000 and an annualized rate of occurrence of 0.25. What is the annualized loss expectancy?
questions.explanation: Annualized loss expectancy equals single loss expectancy multiplied by annualized rate of occurrence: $80,000 × 0.25 = $20,000. The other values result from using an incorrect operation or treating the expected frequency as if one loss occurred every year. ALE is an estimate used to compare risk and treatment costs, not a guarantee of actual loss.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Selecting an appropriate risk treatment strategy
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize risk avoidance when an activity is discontinued
questions.scenarioContext: A media firm considers offering a service in a region where the required operating model would exceed the firm's approved risk appetite. Leadership decides not to launch the service there.
questions.prompt: Which risk treatment strategy has leadership selected?

choices.A: Acceptance
choices.B: Avoidance
choices.C: Mitigation
choices.D: Transfer

questions.explanation: The firm avoids the risk by choosing not to undertake the activity that would create the exposure. Acceptance would retain the risk, mitigation would reduce its likelihood or impact while continuing the activity, and transfer would shift defined financial consequences through a contract or insurance without removing organizational accountability.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Using risk appetite and tolerance to escalate risk decisions
questions.performanceIndicator: Determine the correct governance response when residual risk exceeds delegated authority
questions.scenarioContext: After a mitigation project, the residual risk to a clinical scheduling service remains above the approved tolerance. The service manager's delegated acceptance authority covers only risks within tolerance, and suspending the service could disrupt patient care.
questions.prompt: What should the service manager do NEXT?

choices.A: Accept the risk because mitigation has already been attempted
choices.B: Alter the risk rating so it falls within delegated authority
choices.C: Escalate the decision with treatment options and business-impact information to an authorized risk owner
choices.D: Immediately suspend the service without consulting business continuity stakeholders

questions.explanation: Residual risk above tolerance must be escalated to someone authorized to decide whether to add treatment, change the activity, or formally approve an exception. A prior mitigation attempt does not create acceptance authority, and changing the rating would undermine governance. Immediate suspension may itself create serious business harm and should be evaluated by accountable stakeholders unless an emergency mandate requires it.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Applying STRIDE categories during threat modeling
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify spoofing and tampering threats from concise system behaviors
questions.prompt: During STRIDE threat modeling, the team identifies an attacker impersonating a trusted service account and separately changing a transaction while it is stored. Which 2 STRIDE categories correspond to these threats? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Spoofing
choices.B: Tampering
choices.C: Repudiation
choices.D: Information disclosure
choices.E: Denial of service

questions.explanation: Impersonating a trusted identity is spoofing, while unauthorized modification of stored transaction data is tampering. Repudiation concerns denying an action, information disclosure concerns unauthorized exposure, and denial of service concerns loss or degradation of availability. Those categories do not directly describe the two behaviors stated.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Establishing risk-based vendor requirements before contracting
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize third-party assessment and enforceable requirements during procurement
questions.scenarioContext: A logistics company is selecting a provider that will process sensitive shipment and customer data. Procurement has compared price and features but has not assessed security or included security terms in the draft agreement.
questions.prompt: What should the security manager recommend BEFORE contract execution?

choices.A: Rely on the provider's marketing statement as evidence of adequate security
choices.B: Perform a risk-based assessment and add measurable security, notification, audit, and service requirements
choices.C: Accept all provider risk because outsourcing transfers accountability
choices.D: Wait for the first service review to determine whether contractual requirements are needed

questions.explanation: Due diligence before signing should evaluate the provider's risk and convert important expectations into enforceable, measurable contract and service terms. Marketing claims are insufficient evidence. Outsourcing may allocate certain obligations or financial consequences, but the customer retains accountability for managing its risk. Post-contract review is too late to negotiate essential protections effectively.

questions.competency: I.C — Risk Management Concepts, Threat Modeling, and Supply Chain Risk
questions.skill: Monitoring changes in enterprise risk over time
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose indicators that support actionable risk reporting and escalation
questions.scenarioContext: A financial cooperative maintains a risk register, but senior leaders receive only a quarterly count of open technical findings. They cannot tell whether exposure is rising, whether treatment is late, or whether risk is approaching tolerance limits.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would provide the MOST useful risk oversight?

choices.A: Report trends in key risk indicators, residual risk, treatment status, ownership, and tolerance breaches
choices.B: Replace risk reporting with a complete list of raw event logs
choices.C: Report only findings that have already caused a confirmed loss
choices.D: Remove accepted risks from all future monitoring

questions.explanation: Decision-makers need contextual, trend-based information showing residual exposure, accountable owners, treatment progress, and movement toward or beyond tolerance. Raw logs are too operational for enterprise oversight, confirmed losses are lagging and incomplete indicators, and accepted risk must still be monitored because assumptions and conditions can change.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Using a business impact analysis to establish recovery priorities
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the analysis that must precede solution selection in continuity planning
questions.scenarioContext: A regional wholesaler is updating its continuity program. Technology teams want to purchase recovery services immediately, but the organization has not identified critical processes, dependencies, outage impacts, or acceptable recovery timeframes.
questions.prompt: What should the continuity manager do FIRST?

choices.A: Select the recovery service with the shortest advertised restoration time
choices.B: Conduct a business impact analysis with process owners
choices.C: Copy the disaster recovery plan used by the largest business unit
choices.D: Ask technology teams to assign priorities based only on system cost

questions.explanation: A business impact analysis identifies critical activities, dependencies, consequences of disruption, and recovery requirements so strategies can be selected rationally. Buying a solution first may misalign cost and capability. Reusing one unit's plan ignores enterprise differences, and system cost alone does not reveal business criticality or acceptable downtime.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Designing secure employee termination procedures
questions.performanceIndicator: Coordinate access removal, asset recovery, and continuing obligations for a high-risk departure
questions.scenarioContext: A privileged database administrator will be involuntarily terminated at a scheduled meeting tomorrow. Human resources has notified security under an approved confidential process.
questions.prompt: Which plan BEST reduces risk while supporting a controlled termination?

choices.A: Disable access at a coordinated time, recover organizational assets, preserve needed records, and remind the employee of continuing obligations
choices.B: Disable access now without coordinating with human resources or the administrator's manager
choices.C: Leave access active for several days so the employee can answer follow-up questions
choices.D: Delete the administrator's account and all associated activity records during the meeting

questions.explanation: A coordinated termination synchronizes access revocation with the meeting, recovers assets, preserves evidence and business records, and reinforces confidentiality or other surviving obligations. Premature unilateral revocation can disrupt the planned process, delayed access creates avoidable exposure, and deleting records can harm operations, investigations, and retention compliance.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Designing role-based security education and training
questions.performanceIndicator: Differentiate broad awareness from training tailored to job responsibilities
questions.scenarioContext: An engineering firm gives every worker the same annual security awareness presentation. Developers continue to introduce preventable security defects, even though completion rates are high.
questions.prompt: Which change is MOST likely to address the weakness?

choices.A: Increase the length of the same general presentation for all employees
choices.B: Add role-based secure development training with practical exercises and outcome measures
choices.C: Measure success only by whether employees opened the presentation
choices.D: Replace training with a policy requiring defect-free software

questions.explanation: General awareness builds broad recognition, while developers need role-based knowledge and practiced skills tied to their responsibilities. Practical exercises and outcome measures can reveal whether behavior and capability improve. A longer generic presentation does not address the skill gap, opening content is not evidence of learning, and policy alone cannot build competence.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Establishing personnel security controls for contractors
questions.performanceIndicator: Select complementary pre-access and end-of-engagement controls
questions.scenarioContext: A research organization will give temporary contractors access to confidential project information. The engagement lasts three months and access should end immediately when each assignment concludes.
questions.prompt: Which 2 controls are MOST important to establish for this engagement? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Risk-appropriate screening and signed confidentiality terms before access is granted
choices.B: Documented sponsorship, access expiration, and prompt offboarding tied to the assignment end date
choices.C: Permanent access so returning contractors can resume work quickly
choices.D: An informal verbal agreement that replaces written security requirements
choices.E: A single shared account to simplify contractor administration

questions.explanation: Risk-appropriate screening and enforceable confidentiality terms establish trust and obligations before access. Sponsorship, defined expiration, and prompt offboarding limit access to the authorized engagement. Permanent access violates least privilege, verbal arrangements provide weak governance, and shared accounts undermine accountability and controlled revocation.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Interpreting recovery objectives during business continuity planning
questions.performanceIndicator: Distinguish maximum tolerable downtime from a planned recovery target
questions.scenarioContext: A billing process becomes unacceptable to the business after 12 hours of disruption. The continuity team sets a target to restore the supporting service within 8 hours, leaving time for validation and process recovery.
questions.prompt: How should the 8-hour target be interpreted?

choices.A: It is the recovery time objective, set shorter than the maximum tolerable downtime
choices.B: It is the annualized rate of occurrence for the disruption
choices.C: It is the recovery point objective for allowable data loss
choices.D: It is proof that the process will always recover within 8 hours

questions.explanation: The recovery time objective is the planned target for restoring a service after disruption and should support recovery before the maximum tolerable downtime is reached. Annualized rate of occurrence is a risk-frequency estimate. Recovery point objective measures tolerable data loss in time, and an objective is a planning requirement rather than a guarantee of actual performance.

questions.competency: I.D — Business Continuity, Personnel Security, and Security Awareness Programs
questions.skill: Evaluating the effectiveness of a security awareness program
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose measures that demonstrate behavioral and risk improvement
questions.scenarioContext: A public utility reports that 99 percent of personnel completed required awareness content. Its board asks whether the program actually reduces human-related risk rather than merely documenting attendance.
questions.prompt: Which measurement approach would BEST answer the board's question?

choices.A: Track only annual completion percentages because completion proves behavioral change
choices.B: Compare role-relevant simulations, incident trends, reporting behavior, and targeted knowledge results over time
choices.C: Count the number of slides included in each awareness course
choices.D: Ask course authors whether they believe the material is effective

questions.explanation: A combination of behavioral, operational, and knowledge measures tracked over time provides stronger evidence that awareness changes actions and reduces risk. Completion is useful for compliance but does not prove effectiveness. Content volume is not an outcome, and author opinion lacks the objective evidence needed for governance decisions.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Assigning classification based on business impact
questions.performanceIndicator: Determine an appropriate classification from sensitivity, criticality, and business-impact criteria
questions.scenarioContext: A regional manufacturer is classifying the configuration files used by its automated production lines. Unauthorized disclosure would reveal little of value, but unauthorized modification or loss of availability could stop production and create unsafe operating conditions.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST basis for assigning the classification and handling requirements for these files?

choices.A: Classify them at a low level because their confidentiality impact is limited.
choices.B: Classify them according to the highest relevant business impact, including integrity and availability.
choices.C: Use the classification assigned to the servers on which the files are stored.
choices.D: Delay classification until a production interruption demonstrates the actual impact.

questions.explanation: Classification should reflect all relevant impact dimensions, not confidentiality alone. The severe integrity and availability consequences justify handling requirements aligned with the highest applicable business impact. Inheriting a server label may ignore the files' actual value, and waiting for an incident is reactive rather than risk-based.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Distinguishing data owner and custodian accountability
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the role accountable for approving classification and access requirements
questions.scenarioContext: During an access review, the infrastructure team asks whether archived customer records may be made available to a new analytics group. The infrastructure team operates the storage platform, while the customer-service executive is accountable for the records and their business use.
questions.prompt: Who should make the authorization decision?

choices.A: The data custodian, because that role implements storage and access controls
choices.B: The data owner, because that role determines classification and authorized use
choices.C: The data processor, because that role performs operations on the records
choices.D: The data steward, because that role maintains data definitions and quality

questions.explanation: The data owner is accountable for determining appropriate use, classification, and access to the records. The custodian implements the approved controls but should not independently authorize a new business use. A processor handles data on another party's behalf, while a steward generally supports quality, definitions, and governance execution rather than owning this authorization decision.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Maintaining classification through information aggregation
questions.performanceIndicator: Evaluate whether combined data changes sensitivity and handling requirements
questions.scenarioContext: A public-sector research unit combines three datasets that are each approved for internal use. The merged dataset makes it possible to infer the identities and locations of individuals, even though none of the source datasets reveals both elements by itself.
questions.prompt: What should the security manager do FIRST?

choices.A: Retain the internal-use label because every source dataset already has that label.
choices.B: Reassess the merged dataset and assign handling requirements based on the new aggregate sensitivity.
choices.C: Remove the source labels because aggregation creates a new asset with no inherited restrictions.
choices.D: Permit unrestricted sharing until the data owner documents a confirmed disclosure event.

questions.explanation: Aggregation can create sensitivity that is not present in the individual sources, so the merged asset requires a new classification assessment before use or sharing. Simply retaining or removing the original labels fails to evaluate the inference risk. Waiting for an actual disclosure would expose the organization to avoidable harm.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Applying handling rules when transferring classified information
questions.performanceIndicator: Select handling safeguards that follow the asset's classification across locations
questions.scenarioContext: An engineering firm permits restricted design documents to be viewed only in managed environments. A project leader wants to send one of these documents to an approved contractor whose personal file-sharing account is convenient but is not covered by the firm's handling standard.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST response?

choices.A: Allow the transfer because the contractor is already approved for the project.
choices.B: Lower the document's classification temporarily so the transfer can proceed.
choices.C: Use an approved transfer method that enforces the document's existing handling requirements.
choices.D: Send the document after the contractor agrees verbally not to redistribute it.

questions.explanation: Authorization to participate in a project does not remove the handling controls attached to a restricted asset. The transfer should use an approved method that maintains those controls. Convenience, a temporary relabeling, or a verbal assurance does not provide the required protection or formally change the asset's sensitivity.

questions.competency: II.A — Classifying and Handling Information and Assets
questions.skill: Separating controller and processor responsibilities
questions.performanceIndicator: Differentiate accountability for determining processing purposes from responsibility for following documented instructions
questions.scenarioContext: A subscription service determines why and how customer profile data will be used. It hires a service provider to process that data solely under documented instructions. The organization is defining responsibilities before the service begins.
questions.prompt: Which TWO responsibility assignments are most appropriate? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: The subscription service, as data controller, determines the purposes and essential means of processing.
choices.B: The service provider, as data processor, may independently expand the processing purpose when it improves efficiency.
choices.C: The service provider, as data processor, follows documented instructions and applies the required safeguards.
choices.D: The data custodian becomes the controller because it operates the storage infrastructure.
choices.E: The business owner transfers all accountability for the data when the processing contract is signed.

questions.explanation: The controller determines the purposes and essential means of processing, while the processor acts on the controller's documented instructions and implements required protections. A processor cannot unilaterally create a new purpose merely for efficiency. Operating storage does not by itself make a custodian the controller, and contracting does not eliminate the organization's accountability.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Applying secure provisioning before asset deployment
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify prerequisite lifecycle controls for newly acquired hardware
questions.scenarioContext: A logistics company receives network-connected warehouse scanners that must be placed into service quickly. The devices arrive with vendor defaults, unverified software versions, and no entries in the organization's asset inventory.
questions.prompt: What should occur BEFORE the scanners are connected to the production network?

choices.A: Record, validate, securely configure, and formally authorize the devices through the provisioning process.
choices.B: Connect the devices temporarily and document them after operational testing is complete.
choices.C: Allow warehouse supervisors to select settings because they understand the workflow.
choices.D: Rely on the vendor defaults until the first scheduled annual control review.

questions.explanation: Secure provisioning establishes inventory, validates the asset and its software, applies approved configurations, and authorizes deployment before production exposure. Connecting first creates an unmanaged risk window. Operational knowledge does not replace security baselines, and vendor defaults should not be assumed to meet organizational requirements.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Minimizing risk through defensible retention periods
questions.performanceIndicator: Balance legal, regulatory, contractual, and business requirements when setting retention
questions.scenarioContext: A financial cooperative keeps every customer document indefinitely because storage is inexpensive. Counsel confirms that several record categories have defined minimum retention periods, but no requirement applies after those periods and the business has no documented continuing need.
questions.prompt: Which recommendation BEST reduces risk while meeting obligations?

choices.A: Keep all records indefinitely to maximize the information available for future analysis.
choices.B: Delete every record immediately after the legal minimum period, regardless of other needs.
choices.C: Create category-specific schedules that retain records only for validated legal and business needs, then dispose of them securely.
choices.D: Let each employee decide when records under that employee's control no longer appear useful.

questions.explanation: Category-specific schedules provide a defensible balance among legal, regulatory, contractual, and documented business needs while limiting unnecessary exposure. Indefinite retention enlarges the breach, discovery, and management burden. Automatic deletion at the minimum may ignore valid holds or business needs, while individual discretion produces inconsistent and unauditable outcomes.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Deprovisioning personnel-related assets after role change
questions.performanceIndicator: Coordinate prompt removal and reassignment of assets when employment status changes
questions.scenarioContext: A laboratory employee transfers to a nontechnical department. The identity system updates the employee's primary job role, but specialized software licenses, laboratory devices, local data copies, and issued media remain assigned to the employee.
questions.prompt: What is the MOST important improvement to the asset lifecycle process?

choices.A: Wait for the annual inventory so the remaining assets can be reconciled in one batch.
choices.B: Trigger a role-change workflow that reviews, revokes, returns, sanitizes, or reassigns all associated assets.
choices.C: Ask the employee to retain the assets in case the original department needs temporary assistance.
choices.D: Update only the software inventory because physical assets are controlled by building access.

questions.explanation: A role change should trigger coordinated deprovisioning across logical, physical, software, media, and data assets. This reduces excess access, licensing, loss, and data-exposure risks promptly. Annual reconciliation is too late, retaining assets for convenience preserves unnecessary risk, and building access does not adequately control assigned devices or local copies.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Preserving records subject to a legal hold
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize when normal disposition must be suspended for specifically affected records
questions.scenarioContext: A construction company receives notice of litigation involving one completed project. Its approved schedule calls for routine deletion of project correspondence at the end of the month, including messages related to that project.
questions.prompt: What should the records manager do FIRST?

choices.A: Suspend disposition for records within the hold's scope and preserve them in a controlled manner.
choices.B: Suspend deletion of every record in the company until the litigation is fully resolved.
choices.C: Continue the approved schedule because changing it would make retention inconsistent.
choices.D: Allow project staff to choose which messages appear relevant enough to preserve.

questions.explanation: A legal hold overrides normal disposition for records within its defined scope, which must be identified and preserved under controlled procedures. Freezing all organizational records is unnecessarily broad unless the hold requires it. Continuing deletion risks spoliation, while leaving relevance decisions solely to project staff produces incomplete and inconsistent preservation.

questions.competency: II.B — Secure Provisioning and Asset Retention
questions.skill: Controlling software assets from acquisition through retirement
questions.performanceIndicator: Select lifecycle governance that maintains authorization, supportability, and inventory accuracy
questions.scenarioContext: An educational institution discovers that departments independently acquire software, keep unsupported versions, and retain installation packages after the related systems are retired. Security cannot reliably determine which applications are authorized or still required.
questions.prompt: Which control would BEST address the underlying problem?

choices.A: A centralized software asset lifecycle process covering approval, inventory, maintenance, and retirement
choices.B: A quarterly reminder asking employees to remove applications they no longer use
choices.C: A larger storage allocation so departments can preserve every software version
choices.D: An incident response procedure focused on malware found on unsupported systems

questions.explanation: The root issue is missing governance across acquisition, deployment, maintenance, and retirement. A centralized lifecycle process creates authoritative inventory and control over authorization and support status. Reminders depend on inconsistent individual action, additional storage reinforces over-retention, and incident response treats consequences rather than the provisioning problem.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Protecting data during the sharing stage
questions.performanceIndicator: Tailor data controls to classification, recipient, purpose, and transfer path
questions.scenarioContext: A health-research organization must provide a limited dataset to an external research partner for an approved study. The complete internal dataset contains additional sensitive fields that the partner does not need.
questions.prompt: Which approach BEST addresses security during the sharing stage of the data lifecycle?

choices.A: Provide the complete dataset because contractual approval establishes a trusted relationship.
choices.B: Share only the necessary fields through an approved channel under documented use and handling restrictions.
choices.C: Move the complete dataset to an archive before giving the partner access to it.
choices.D: Allow the partner to select and delete unnecessary fields after receiving the complete dataset.

questions.explanation: The best approach combines data minimization with an approved transfer path and explicit use and handling constraints. A trusted or contracted recipient should still receive only what is necessary. Archiving does not reduce the disclosed content, and asking the recipient to remove excess fields exposes those fields before minimization occurs.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Selecting media sanitization based on reuse and assurance needs
questions.performanceIndicator: Match clearing, purging, or destruction to media disposition and data sensitivity
questions.scenarioContext: A defense supplier plans to release failed solid-state drives that held highly sensitive design data to an external recycling firm. The drives cannot be reliably accessed to perform or verify a supported purge operation.
questions.prompt: What is the MOST appropriate disposition method?

choices.A: Clear the drives using a standard file-deletion utility.
choices.B: Reformat the drives and confirm that no filenames remain visible.
choices.C: Physically destroy the drives using an approved, verifiable process before release.
choices.D: Transfer the drives intact after obtaining a confidentiality agreement from the recycler.

questions.explanation: Because the media is leaving organizational control, contains highly sensitive data, and cannot be reliably purged, approved physical destruction provides the appropriate assurance against remanence. File deletion and reformatting are forms of logical clearing that may leave recoverable data. A confidentiality agreement does not substitute for sanitization.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Using data loss prevention to enforce handling policy
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify a control that detects and restricts unauthorized movement of classified data
questions.scenarioContext: A consulting firm labels client reports as restricted, yet employees can still copy report contents into personal webmail or removable media. Management wants a control that can identify the sensitive content and enforce policy at common exit points.
questions.prompt: Which technology BEST meets this requirement?

choices.A: Digital rights management that controls permitted use of designated documents
choices.B: Data loss prevention that inspects content and applies policy to attempted transfers
choices.C: A cloud access security broker limited to inventorying sanctioned cloud subscriptions
choices.D: A records archive that preserves reports after their active use ends

questions.explanation: Data loss prevention is designed to discover sensitive content and monitor or block its movement through endpoints, messaging, and network channels according to policy. Digital rights management can constrain use of protected files but is not the best general control for inspecting copied content across exit points. Cloud inventory and archiving address different lifecycle needs.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Selecting layered controls for cloud data use and sharing
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose complementary technologies that protect classified data across lifecycle activities
questions.scenarioContext: A media company is adopting multiple cloud collaboration services. It needs visibility into cloud use, enforcement of data-handling policy when users upload sensitive material, and persistent restrictions on how authorized recipients can use selected documents after delivery.
questions.prompt: Which THREE controls most directly address these requirements? Select 3 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: A cloud access security broker for visibility and policy enforcement across cloud services
choices.B: Data loss prevention for detecting sensitive content and controlling uploads
choices.C: Digital rights management for persistent restrictions on designated documents
choices.D: A longer retention schedule for all collaboration records
choices.E: A hardware inventory reconciliation for employee workstations

questions.explanation: A cloud access security broker provides cloud-use visibility and policy enforcement, data loss prevention detects sensitive content and can restrict uploads, and digital rights management maintains usage restrictions on protected documents. Extending retention does not control current cloud movement or recipient actions, and workstation inventory does not directly address the stated data-protection requirements.

questions.competency: II.C — The Data Lifecycle and Data Security Controls
questions.skill: Scoping and tailoring controls for data in use
questions.performanceIndicator: Adapt baseline controls to a processing context without weakening stated protection objectives
questions.scenarioContext: A utility company applies a corporate data-protection baseline to office systems and an operational analytics platform. One baseline control cannot be implemented on the analytics platform as written because it would interrupt time-critical processing. The data remains sensitive while being processed.
questions.prompt: What should the security architect recommend?

choices.A: Exclude the platform from the baseline because availability has priority in operational environments.
choices.B: Accept the missing control informally because the platform team understands the operational risk.
choices.C: Tailor the control through the approved risk process and implement compensating protection that meets the security objective.
choices.D: Apply the control unchanged and treat any processing interruption as an operational issue.

questions.explanation: Control tailoring should occur through an authorized, documented risk process and preserve the original protection objective through suitable compensating measures. A blanket exclusion or informal acceptance leaves sensitive data in use inadequately governed. Applying the baseline without considering operational constraints may create unacceptable availability consequences rather than balancing the full risk context.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Applying fail-secure design to an access-control dependency
questions.performanceIndicator: Select an architecture that preserves confidentiality when a supporting service fails
questions.scenarioContext: A research organization is designing a laboratory records system. Authorization decisions depend on a separate policy service, and the records are highly confidential.
questions.prompt: If the policy service becomes unavailable, which system behavior BEST implements the fail-secure principle?

choices.A: Permit all authenticated users until the policy service recovers.
choices.B: Retain each user's most permissive authorization from the prior session.
choices.C: Deny new access requests while preserving only explicitly approved emergency procedures.
choices.D: Disable audit logging to reduce demand on the remaining services.

questions.explanation: Denying new requests places the system in a secure state when it cannot obtain an authorization decision, while a separately approved emergency procedure can address availability needs. Permitting access or retaining the most permissive prior state could expose confidential records. Disabling logging weakens accountability and does not solve the authorization failure.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Selecting a formal security model for confidentiality requirements
questions.performanceIndicator: Match mandatory confidentiality rules to the appropriate formal model
questions.scenarioContext: A government contractor must prevent analysts from reading information above their clearance and from writing classified information into a lower classification level.
questions.prompt: Which formal security model MOST directly supports these requirements?

choices.A: Bell-LaPadula
choices.B: Biba
choices.C: Clark-Wilson
choices.D: Brewer-Nash

questions.explanation: Bell-LaPadula is designed to protect confidentiality through rules commonly summarized as no read up and no write down. Biba focuses on integrity, Clark-Wilson emphasizes well-formed transactions and separation of duties, and Brewer-Nash addresses conflicts of interest through dynamic access restrictions.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Applying separation of duties to high-risk administrative changes
questions.performanceIndicator: Design a control workflow that prevents unilateral privileged actions
questions.scenarioContext: A financial services firm found that one infrastructure administrator can request, approve, and implement changes to the hardware root of trust used by critical servers.
questions.prompt: Which redesign BEST applies separation of duties while retaining operational accountability?

choices.A: Rotate the administrator's password after each approved change.
choices.B: Require an independent approver and separate implementation role, with attributable audit records.
choices.C: Allow the administrator to proceed after documenting the business reason in a personal log.
choices.D: Grant the same end-to-end privileges to a backup administrator for availability.

questions.explanation: Splitting approval and implementation between accountable individuals prevents one person from completing the entire sensitive transaction and creates traceable oversight. Password rotation does not separate authority. A personal log is not independent approval, and duplicating the same end-to-end privilege preserves the original control weakness.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Choosing hardware protection for high-value cryptographic keys
questions.performanceIndicator: Differentiate hardware security modules from platform integrity components
questions.scenarioContext: An online payment service needs centralized generation, storage, and use of private signing keys. The keys must remain nonexportable, and cryptographic operations require strict administrative controls.
questions.prompt: Which security capability is the MOST appropriate foundation for this requirement?

choices.A: A hardware security module with controlled key operations
choices.B: A trusted platform module installed in each employee workstation
choices.C: Encrypted application configuration files stored with the servers
choices.D: Process isolation within the payment application's operating system

questions.explanation: A hardware security module is designed to generate, protect, and use high-value keys inside a tamper-resistant boundary with controlled administration. A trusted platform module primarily supports the integrity and key needs of its host device. Encrypted configuration files still expose keys to host processes, while process isolation alone does not provide equivalent key custody.

questions.competency: III.A — Secure Design Principles, Security Models, Control Selection, and System Security Capabilities
questions.skill: Identifying zero trust architecture principles
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize design choices that reduce implicit trust and limit compromise
questions.scenarioContext: A media company is redesigning an internal application environment after learning that network location is treated as sufficient evidence of trust.
questions.prompt: Which TWO design changes BEST align with zero trust principles? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Authorize each request using current identity, device, and resource context.
choices.B: Place all internal applications on one trusted network segment.
choices.C: Grant broad access after a user successfully connects to the corporate network.
choices.D: Continuously evaluate access signals and restrict privileges to required resources.
choices.E: Replace application authorization with perimeter firewall rules.

questions.explanation: Context-aware authorization for each request and continuous evaluation with least privilege directly reduce implicit trust. A single trusted segment and broad post-connection access preserve location-based trust. Perimeter rules remain useful controls but cannot replace resource-level authorization in a zero trust design.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Mitigating safety and availability risks in industrial control systems
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize architecture changes appropriate for legacy operational technology
questions.scenarioContext: A water treatment facility operates legacy controllers that cannot support endpoint agents or frequent patching. A recent review found direct routable connectivity between office workstations and the control environment.
questions.prompt: Which architectural change should the security architect recommend FIRST?

choices.A: Replace every controller immediately with a general-purpose server.
choices.B: Segment the control environment and tightly mediate required communications through monitored boundaries.
choices.C: Install the corporate endpoint agent on every controller despite compatibility concerns.
choices.D: Increase password complexity on office workstations without changing connectivity.

questions.explanation: Segmentation with controlled, monitored communication paths reduces exposure without disrupting fragile controllers and is a strong first architectural control. Immediate wholesale replacement may create safety and availability risk. Unsupported agents can impair operations, while office password changes do not address the direct network path into the control environment.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Reducing container escape and shared-kernel risk
questions.performanceIndicator: Select layered controls for hostile multitenant container workloads
questions.scenarioContext: A development platform will execute untrusted customer workloads in containers. The security team is concerned that a container escape could expose other tenants because containers share the host kernel.
questions.prompt: Which design MOST effectively addresses the stated risk?

choices.A: Run every container with privileged mode enabled for compatibility.
choices.B: Use hardened minimal hosts, unprivileged containers, mandatory isolation controls, and stronger workload boundaries where required.
choices.C: Scan approved container images before deployment but leave runtime privileges and host settings unchanged.
choices.D: Assign separate application credentials to each tenant while retaining the shared default kernel configuration.

questions.explanation: Hardened hosts, reduced container privilege, enforced isolation, and stronger boundaries for higher-risk workloads provide defense in depth against shared-kernel compromise. Privileged containers increase exposure, a shared writable registry creates supply-chain risk, and application passwords do not isolate kernel resources.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Applying the cloud shared responsibility model to platform services
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify customer responsibilities in a managed application platform
questions.scenarioContext: A retailer deploys an application on a managed platform service. The provider maintains the physical infrastructure, virtualization layer, operating system, and platform runtime.
questions.prompt: Which responsibility MOST clearly remains with the retailer?

choices.A: Replacing failed disks in the provider's data center
choices.B: Patching the provider-managed hypervisor
choices.C: Securing application code, identities, configuration, and customer data
choices.D: Maintaining the provider's physical perimeter controls

questions.explanation: In a managed platform model, the customer remains responsible for its application, identities, configurations, and data even when the provider operates lower layers. Physical facilities, disks, and the provider-managed hypervisor are provider responsibilities. Exact allocations should still be confirmed in the service agreement.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Protecting constrained Internet of Things devices through compensating architecture
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose controls that reduce exposure when embedded devices cannot be remediated directly
questions.scenarioContext: A hospital uses network-connected environmental sensors with fixed firmware and hard-coded service credentials. Replacement is scheduled but will take nine months, and the devices need to send readings only to one collection service.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST interim architectural mitigation?

choices.A: Place the sensors on a restricted segment that permits only necessary traffic to the collection service and monitors anomalies.
choices.B: Require administrators to use a managed workstation while leaving the sensors on the general user network.
choices.C: Place the sensors behind a gateway that authenticates administrators but permits unrestricted outbound sensor traffic.
choices.D: Increase monitoring of the existing flat network without restricting communication paths.

questions.explanation: A restricted segment with allowlisted communication and monitoring limits both the reach and impact of devices that cannot be secured internally. A managed administrative endpoint improves one access path but leaves the devices broadly exposed. Gateway authentication without outbound restriction and monitoring without segmentation each address only part of the risk.

questions.competency: III.B — Vulnerabilities Across Modern Architectures
questions.skill: Preventing unauthorized database access through service-layer controls
questions.performanceIndicator: Distinguish architectural least privilege from client-side restrictions
questions.scenarioContext: A benefits portal currently allows desktop clients to connect directly to a database using one shared account with broad table permissions.
questions.prompt: Which redesign BEST reduces the architectural vulnerability?

choices.A: Hide the shared database password in the desktop application's compiled code.
choices.B: Route requests through a service layer that validates authorization and uses narrowly scoped database privileges.
choices.C: Rename sensitive tables so users cannot easily identify them.
choices.D: Give each desktop client the shared account through an encrypted configuration file.

questions.explanation: A controlled service layer can enforce business authorization and limit database operations through narrowly scoped identities. Credentials embedded in code or configuration can still be extracted and retain excessive authority. Renaming tables provides obscurity rather than access control.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Selecting cryptographic mechanisms for data integrity and origin assurance
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose a digital signature when both integrity and signer verification are required
questions.scenarioContext: A procurement system sends approved purchase orders to external suppliers. Suppliers must be able to verify that an order was not altered and that it was approved using the organization's controlled private key.
questions.prompt: Which mechanism BEST satisfies both requirements?

choices.A: A digital signature over the purchase order
choices.B: A plain cryptographic hash sent with the purchase order
choices.C: Symmetric encryption using one shared key for every supplier
choices.D: A random salt appended to the purchase order

questions.explanation: A digital signature lets a recipient verify document integrity and validate that the corresponding private key produced the signature. A plain hash detects changes only when its trusted value is delivered separately and does not authenticate the signer. Shared symmetric encryption does not provide the same third-party-verifiable origin assurance, and a salt alone supplies neither property.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Protecting cryptographic keys throughout their lifecycle
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify essential controls for key generation and retirement
questions.scenarioContext: A manufacturer is defining a lifecycle for keys that protect proprietary design archives. The current process permits administrators to generate keys on ordinary workstations and retains retired key copies indefinitely without documented need.
questions.prompt: Which TWO controls would MOST directly improve the cryptographic key lifecycle? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Generate keys using an approved source of cryptographically secure randomness in a controlled environment.
choices.B: Publish private keys with the archive so future users can recover the data.
choices.C: Define retention, archival, revocation, and destruction rules based on data and recovery requirements.
choices.D: Reuse one key across unrelated systems to reduce administrative effort.
choices.E: Extend every key's cryptoperiod whenever rotation creates operational work.

questions.explanation: Secure generation protects keys at creation, while defined archival, revocation, retention, and destruction rules control them through retirement. Publishing private keys destroys confidentiality. Broad reuse increases the effect of compromise, and repeatedly extending cryptoperiods for convenience ignores risk-based lifecycle requirements.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Using salts to protect stored password verifiers
questions.performanceIndicator: Explain how unique salts impede precomputed password attacks
questions.prompt: What is the PRIMARY security benefit of applying a unique random salt to each password before using an appropriate password-hashing function?

choices.A: It makes identical passwords produce different stored values and reduces the usefulness of precomputed tables.
choices.B: It makes weak passwords resistant to every offline guessing attempt.
choices.C: It allows the server to recover the original password when needed.
choices.D: It provides non-repudiation for each successful login.

questions.explanation: A unique salt causes equal passwords to produce different stored verifiers and forces attackers to perform work separately for each salt instead of efficiently reusing precomputed results. Salting does not make weak passwords unguessable, enable password recovery, or create a digital signature that could support non-repudiation.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Responding to certificate authority key compromise
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize trust revocation and controlled certificate replacement
questions.scenarioContext: An enterprise discovers credible evidence that the private signing key of an internal intermediate certificate authority was extracted by an attacker.
questions.prompt: Which response BEST protects relying systems from certificates fraudulently issued under the compromised key?

choices.A: Increase the key length of newly issued end-entity certificates while retaining the intermediate authority.
choices.B: Revoke the compromised intermediate certificate, distribute updated trust and revocation information, and reissue affected certificates under a new protected key.
choices.C: Wait until the intermediate certificate expires to avoid disrupting applications.
choices.D: Change the certificate authority's display name and continue using the existing signing key.

questions.explanation: Revoking the compromised authority and propagating that status removes trust from certificates chained through it; controlled reissuance under a new protected key restores service. Stronger end-entity keys cannot repair a compromised issuer. Waiting leaves fraudulent certificates trusted, and renaming the authority has no cryptographic effect.

questions.competency: III.C — Cryptographic Solutions and Cryptanalytic Attacks
questions.skill: Identifying side-channel leakage from cryptographic implementations
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize attacks based on observable implementation behavior
questions.scenarioContext: A laboratory demonstrates that private-key bits can be inferred by correlating thousands of cryptographic operations with small variations in device power consumption.
questions.prompt: What type of attack does this finding MOST directly demonstrate?

choices.A: Ciphertext-only attack
choices.B: Frequency-analysis attack
choices.C: Side-channel attack
choices.D: Known-plaintext attack

questions.explanation: Power analysis is a side-channel attack because it exploits physical information leaked by an implementation rather than a mathematical weakness in the algorithm. Ciphertext-only and known-plaintext attacks are categorized by the attacker's available cryptographic data. Frequency analysis studies symbol patterns and is not the mechanism described.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Selecting fire suppression appropriate for occupied equipment spaces
questions.performanceIndicator: Balance personnel safety, equipment protection, and fire response
questions.scenarioContext: A data center is redesigning fire protection for an equipment room that technicians routinely occupy. Management wants early warning and suppression that minimizes harm to people and electronic systems.
questions.prompt: Which design is MOST appropriate?

choices.A: Smoke detection combined with a code-compliant pre-action system and an appropriate clean-agent system where justified by risk
choices.B: A total-flooding carbon dioxide system with alarms but no engineered mechanism to prevent discharge while personnel remain inside
choices.C: A conventional wet-pipe sprinkler system selected solely for low installation cost, without evaluating accidental-discharge exposure
choices.D: Heat detection paired with portable extinguishers as the only suppression capability for the entire equipment room

questions.explanation: Early smoke detection plus a properly engineered pre-action system reduces accidental water release, while an appropriate clean agent can protect equipment when risk justifies it; all elements must meet life-safety and code requirements. Carbon dioxide presents a serious life-safety concern in occupied areas. A wet-pipe system chosen without risk analysis may create avoidable exposure, while heat detection and portable extinguishers alone provide insufficient early and automatic protection.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Designing layered physical access controls for a critical room
questions.performanceIndicator: Combine deterrent, preventive, detective, and accountability controls
questions.scenarioContext: A regional utility is building a control room inside an existing operations facility. Tailgating and misuse of valid badges are the primary concerns.
questions.prompt: Which control design BEST addresses both concerns?

choices.A: A standard keyed lock with a sign reminding employees not to share keys
choices.B: An access-controlled vestibule using badge and biometric verification, anti-passback logic, monitoring, and retained access logs
choices.C: A reception desk located at the public entrance with no controls at the control room
choices.D: A shared numeric code changed annually and distributed to all facility personnel

questions.explanation: A controlled vestibule limits passage to one verified person, while badge-plus-biometric checks reduce misuse of a badge and monitoring and logs provide detection and accountability. A key or shared code can be copied or shared. A distant reception desk does not adequately control the critical room itself.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Evaluating environmental risks during facility selection
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify location and utility factors that affect resilient site design
questions.scenarioContext: An organization is comparing locations for a new processing facility that must support critical services during regional disruptions.
questions.prompt: Which TWO factors should receive the GREATEST attention during site selection? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Exposure to hazards such as flooding, wildfire, severe weather, and nearby hazardous operations
choices.B: Availability and independence of power, communications, water, and emergency access routes
choices.C: The site's proximity to the largest current group of office employees
choices.D: The cost of adapting existing interior office space for administrative teams
choices.E: The ability to standardize interior lock hardware with noncritical corporate offices

questions.explanation: Regional and adjacent hazards shape the facility's inherent exposure, while resilient utilities and access determine whether critical services can continue through disruptions. Employee proximity and adaptation cost may affect business planning but do not address the stated resilience objective as directly. Standard lock hardware is secondary to selecting a site with acceptable hazard and infrastructure characteristics.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Integrating physical security requirements into the system lifecycle
questions.performanceIndicator: Address facility dependencies before system design decisions become costly to change
questions.scenarioContext: A project will deploy high-density computing equipment in a converted office area. The system design is nearly complete, but no one has assessed power, cooling, floor loading, fire protection, or physical access zoning.
questions.prompt: What should the security architect recommend as the BEST next step?

choices.A: Complete procurement first and address facility limitations after installation.
choices.B: Perform a multidisciplinary facility risk and capacity assessment before final design approval.
choices.C: Treat the equipment vendor's warranty as acceptance of all environmental risks.
choices.D: Limit the review to cybersecurity configuration because the equipment is already selected.

questions.explanation: A multidisciplinary assessment before design approval can identify safety, availability, and physical security requirements while changes remain feasible. Procurement would prematurely lock in assumptions. A warranty does not transfer all operational risk, and a cybersecurity-only review ignores dependencies that directly affect system reliability and protection.

questions.competency: III.D — Site and Facility Security, and the Information System Lifecycle
questions.skill: Designing secure decommissioning for facility-hosted systems
questions.performanceIndicator: Coordinate media protection, asset accountability, and removal of obsolete access
questions.scenarioContext: A company is closing a branch data room. Servers will be reused, storage media will be disposed of, and the leased space will be returned to the property owner.
questions.prompt: Which decommissioning approach BEST protects information and the former facility?

choices.A: Move reusable servers first and let the property owner discard remaining media and access badges.
choices.B: Inventory assets, apply approved media sanitization or destruction, revoke physical and logical access, remove sensitive markings, and retain evidence of completion.
choices.C: Delete visible files from storage media and leave installed access-control devices unchanged.
choices.D: Rely on the lease termination date to end all personnel and system access automatically.

questions.explanation: A controlled decommissioning process maintains asset accountability, protects residual data, removes obsolete access, and documents completion. Delegating media disposal without control can expose information. Ordinary deletion may leave recoverable data, and lease termination does not automatically revoke credentials or remove sensitive facility artifacts.

questions.competency: IV.A — Network Architecture Fundamentals
questions.skill: Determining visibility limits at different network layers
questions.performanceIndicator: Select a monitoring control that can inspect the information required by the security objective
