questions.scenarioContext: Database administrators at an online retailer use permanently enabled shared administrator credentials for both routine work and emergency changes. Post-incident reviews cannot reliably attribute actions to individuals.
questions.prompt: Which control would BEST reduce the risk while preserving necessary administrative capability?

choices.A: Rotate the shared password monthly and distribute it to all administrators
choices.B: Record only failed commands executed through the shared account
choices.C: Create separate shared accounts for routine and emergency work
choices.D: Issue named accounts with just-in-time elevation, approval, and session logging

questions.explanation: Named accounts with time-limited elevation, approval, and session logging minimize standing privilege while supporting attribution and oversight. Rotating or subdividing shared credentials still prevents individual accountability. Recording only failures omits successful actions, which are often the events most important to an investigation.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Selecting media sanitization based on sensitivity and disposition
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply asset and media handling requirements throughout the disposal lifecycle
questions.scenarioContext: A research organization is retiring failed solid-state drives that stored highly sensitive intellectual property. The drives cannot be reliably accessed to perform logical overwriting and will not be reused.
questions.prompt: What is the MOST appropriate disposition method?

choices.A: Return the drives to general inventory after deleting their asset records
choices.B: Physically destroy the drives using an approved process and retain disposition records
choices.C: Quick-format the drives and donate them to another department
choices.D: Relabel the drives as unclassified before sending them to standard recycling

questions.explanation: Approved physical destruction is appropriate when highly sensitive solid-state media cannot be reliably sanitized and will not be reused; disposition records maintain accountability. Quick formatting does not reliably remove data. Relabeling changes neither the data nor its sensitivity, and deleting asset records before controlled disposition breaks lifecycle tracking.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Coordinating immediate ransomware containment and evidence preservation
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose complementary incident-response actions under operational pressure
questions.scenarioContext: A hospital detects ransomware encrypting files on several workstations. Network telemetry indicates active lateral movement, while unaffected clinical systems remain available. The incident response plan has been activated.
questions.prompt: Which TWO actions should the incident commander prioritize during initial containment? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Isolate affected endpoints and restrict the observed lateral-movement paths
choices.B: Erase every affected endpoint before collecting incident data
choices.C: Preserve relevant volatile data, logs, and forensic evidence through authorized procedures
choices.D: Restore all affected endpoints immediately from the most recent available backup
choices.E: Delay internal reporting until the full root cause has been proven

questions.explanation: Initial containment should limit further spread while preserving evidence needed to determine scope and cause. Immediate erasure destroys evidence. Restoration belongs to recovery and should follow containment and validation of clean backups. Reporting should follow the response plan and applicable obligations; it should not wait for perfect certainty about root cause.

questions.competency: VII.B — Foundational Operations Concepts, Resource Protection, and Incident Management
questions.skill: Converting incident lessons learned into operational improvement
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize corrective actions after incident recovery
questions.scenarioContext: A logistics provider has restored services after a credential-stuffing incident. The post-incident review identifies slow escalation, unclear ownership, and a detection rule that produced an excessive number of low-value alerts.
questions.prompt: Which outcome would provide the GREATEST long-term value from the lessons-learned process?

choices.A: Archive the meeting notes without assigning further work
choices.B: Discipline the first analyst who handled the alert
choices.C: Keep the response plan unchanged to preserve procedural consistency
choices.D: Assign tracked improvements to the playbook, alert logic, ownership, and training

questions.explanation: Lessons learned create value when findings become owned, tracked improvements to people, process, and technology. Archiving notes alone does not reduce recurrence. Blaming one analyst ignores systemic weaknesses, and preserving a demonstrably weak plan sacrifices improvement for superficial consistency.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Using egress controls to disrupt data exfiltration
questions.performanceIndicator: Select a preventive and detective control aligned to observed attack behavior
questions.scenarioContext: A media company discovers that a compromised internal workstation is sending encrypted outbound traffic to an unapproved external destination over a port that is normally allowed. Inbound firewall rules did not prevent the activity.
questions.prompt: Which measure would MOST directly reduce the likelihood of similar exfiltration succeeding?

choices.A: Permit outbound connections only through controlled services and monitor destination behavior
choices.B: Increase the retention period for physical access badge records
choices.C: Move the workstation to a larger network segment
choices.D: Disable all inbound logging at the perimeter

questions.explanation: Controlled egress paths, destination restrictions, and outbound monitoring directly address unauthorized exfiltration even when traffic uses an ordinarily permitted port. Badge retention does not control network transfer. A larger segment can increase exposure, and disabling inbound logging reduces visibility without constraining outbound activity.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Operating deception technology without creating production risk
questions.performanceIndicator: Respond appropriately to activity detected in a honeypot
questions.scenarioContext: A utility operates an isolated honeypot containing no legitimate user data. The monitoring team detects interactive access from an internal network address and observes commands consistent with reconnaissance.
questions.prompt: What should the security operations team do FIRST?

choices.A: Add production credentials to the honeypot to learn which accounts the actor prefers
choices.B: Allow the honeypot unrestricted outbound access so the actor can be followed
choices.C: Validate and escalate the high-fidelity alert while preserving telemetry and containing related risk
choices.D: Ignore the event because honeypots are expected to receive unauthorized traffic

questions.explanation: Legitimate users should not interact with the honeypot, so internal interactive access is a high-value signal that should be validated, escalated, preserved, and investigated for related compromise. Adding real credentials creates unnecessary exposure. Unrestricted outbound access could let the system harm others, while ignoring the event wastes the primary purpose of the deception control.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Prioritizing emergency vulnerability remediation
questions.performanceIndicator: Balance exploitability, exposure, business criticality, and change risk
questions.scenarioContext: A critical vulnerability is being actively exploited. The affected internet-facing service supports revenue processing, and a vendor patch is available but has not completed normal regression testing. A tested network-level mitigation can temporarily block the known exploit path.
questions.prompt: Which response BEST balances immediate risk reduction and service stability?

choices.A: Wait for the next routine maintenance window without changing any controls
choices.B: Apply the temporary mitigation, invoke emergency change procedures, test the patch, and deploy it promptly
choices.C: Install the patch immediately outside all change controls and without a rollback plan
choices.D: Permanently retire the revenue service before evaluating compensating controls

questions.explanation: A validated compensating control can reduce immediate exposure while emergency change procedures accelerate testing and deployment of the durable fix. Waiting leaves an actively exploited service exposed. Uncontrolled installation can create avoidable outages, and permanent retirement is disproportionate when effective mitigation and remediation paths exist.

questions.competency: VII.C — Detection, Prevention, Patch, and Change Management
questions.skill: Maintaining security and recoverability during production changes
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the essential elements of a controlled change
questions.scenarioContext: A system owner requests an urgent production change to resolve recurring performance failures. The technical modification has succeeded in a test environment, but its security impact and production reversal steps have not been documented.
questions.prompt: What should the change authority require BEFORE approving implementation?

choices.A: Document security impact, implementation validation, authorization, and a tested rollback approach
choices.B: Obtain only the developer's verbal assurance that the change is low risk
choices.C: Skip post-implementation review because testing already succeeded
choices.D: Transfer permanent approval authority to the system owner

questions.explanation: A controlled production change requires assessed security impact, defined validation, appropriate authorization, and a viable rollback method. A verbal assurance is not sufficient evidence. Test success does not remove the need to verify production results, and the system owner should not receive unrestricted authority that bypasses governance and separation of duties.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Protecting backups from destructive compromise
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose a backup strategy that supports recoverability after ransomware
questions.scenarioContext: A professional services firm backs up production data continuously to storage reachable with the same administrative credentials used for production. During a ransomware incident, attackers encrypted both production data and the connected backup copies.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would BEST address the demonstrated weakness?

choices.A: Increase backup frequency while retaining the shared credentials
choices.B: Store every backup exclusively on the production network
choices.C: Maintain isolated or immutable backup copies under separate access controls and test restoration
choices.D: Replace restoration testing with checks that backup jobs completed

questions.explanation: Isolated or immutable copies with separate administrative controls limit an attacker's ability to destroy recovery data, while restoration tests confirm that the copies are usable. More frequent backups remain vulnerable if the same compromise can reach them. Production-only storage lacks isolation, and successful job status does not prove recoverability.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Selecting a recovery site based on recovery objectives
questions.performanceIndicator: Match recovery-site readiness to an organization's RTO and cost constraints
questions.scenarioContext: A payment processor requires critical transaction services to resume within one hour of a primary-site loss. Management accepts the cost of continuously maintained duplicate infrastructure and near-real-time data replication.
questions.prompt: Which recovery strategy BEST satisfies these requirements?

choices.A: A cold site with power and floor space but no installed processing equipment
choices.B: A warm site requiring hardware configuration and restoration from shipped media
choices.C: A reciprocal agreement to use another organization's spare capacity when available
choices.D: A mirrored site with synchronized systems and rapid failover capability

questions.explanation: A mirrored site provides the continuously maintained infrastructure and synchronized data needed for a very short recovery time objective. Cold and warm sites require substantial activation and restoration time. A reciprocal agreement may lack guaranteed capacity and typically cannot assure the readiness required for critical transaction processing.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Distinguishing parallel disaster recovery testing
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify the operational characteristics and safeguards of a parallel test
questions.scenarioContext: A public agency wants to demonstrate that its alternate processing environment can run recovered applications using restored data. The production environment must remain active and continue serving the public throughout the exercise.
questions.prompt: Which TWO characteristics describe the MOST appropriate disaster recovery test? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Recovery systems are activated and operated alongside production systems
choices.B: Production processing is deliberately shut down and transferred completely
choices.C: The exercise is limited to reading the plan individually without discussion
choices.D: Restored processing is validated without making it the live production service
choices.E: Participants discuss actions around a table without activating recovery systems

questions.explanation: A parallel test activates recovery resources and validates restored processing while the production environment continues to operate. Completely shutting down and transferring production describes a full interruption test. Individual reading and discussion-based exercises provide less operational assurance because they do not activate the recovery systems.

questions.competency: VII.D — Recovery Strategies and Disaster Recovery Processes
questions.skill: Authorizing a high-risk full interruption recovery test
questions.performanceIndicator: Evaluate readiness and risk controls before disruptive disaster recovery testing
questions.scenarioContext: An energy distributor proposes its first full interruption test for a critical business system. Walkthroughs and simulations have found unresolved recovery procedure gaps, and the business has not approved an outage window.
questions.prompt: What should the security manager recommend?

choices.A: Proceed immediately because full interruption testing automatically corrects procedural gaps
choices.B: Resolve material gaps, obtain business authorization, define rollback criteria, and then schedule the test
choices.C: Cancel all future recovery exercises because critical systems should not be tested
choices.D: Perform the interruption without notifying system owners to make the test more realistic

questions.explanation: A full interruption test can provide strong assurance but also creates real operational risk. Material deficiencies should be corrected, accountable business owners must authorize the outage, and rollback and stop criteria should be established before proceeding. An interruption does not fix gaps by itself, permanent avoidance leaves recovery unvalidated, and an unannounced disruption lacks responsible authorization.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Validating continuity arrangements for a critical third-party dependency
questions.performanceIndicator: Use exercises to test business workarounds and dependency assumptions
questions.scenarioContext: A food distributor depends on one external logistics provider for time-sensitive deliveries. The business continuity plan states that staff will switch to an alternate provider during a regional disruption, but the alternate has never participated in an exercise.
questions.prompt: Which action would provide the MOST useful assurance?

choices.A: Conduct an exercise that validates contacts, capacity, data exchange, decision authority, and the alternate workflow
choices.B: Assume the alternate provider can accept the workload because a contract exists
choices.C: Test only the security team's incident notification tree
choices.D: Remove logistics from the continuity plan because the service is outsourced

questions.explanation: A realistic exercise should validate that the alternate arrangement works end to end, including capacity, communications, information exchange, authority, and operational procedures. A contract alone does not prove readiness. Testing only security notifications misses the business process, while outsourcing transfers service delivery but not the organization's continuity responsibility.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Applying layered physical security to restricted internal space
questions.performanceIndicator: Select controls that deter, detect, delay, and support response
questions.scenarioContext: A biotechnology company has strong perimeter access control, but employees from unrestricted office areas can enter a sensitive laboratory by following an authorized worker through an internal door. Investigations show that the door does not reliably latch and no alert is generated when it remains open.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would BEST address the immediate physical security weakness?

choices.A: Add more exterior landscaping around the building
choices.B: Require stronger passwords for laboratory workstations
choices.C: Install controlled individual entry with door-position monitoring and anti-tailgating procedures
choices.D: Extend visitor parking farther from the main entrance

questions.explanation: Controlled individual entry, reliable door-state monitoring, and anti-tailgating procedures directly address unauthorized passage from a general area into the restricted laboratory. Landscaping and parking changes focus on the outer perimeter, not the internal boundary. Strong workstation passwords are useful logical controls but do not prevent unauthorized physical entry.

questions.competency: VII.E — Business Continuity Planning, Physical Security, and Personnel Safety
questions.skill: Protecting personnel during a coercion event
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize life safety and discreet emergency escalation under duress
questions.scenarioContext: A branch employee who handles sensitive records may be forced by an aggressor to request after-hours access. The organization wants a control that alerts responders without requiring the employee to openly resist or escalate the confrontation.
questions.prompt: Which control BEST meets the objective?

choices.A: A rehearsed duress signal that silently alerts designated responders under a documented safety procedure
choices.B: A policy requiring the employee to physically prevent access in every circumstance
choices.C: A public announcement identifying the employee and suspected aggressor
choices.D: A quarterly report listing all ordinary after-hours access requests

questions.explanation: A discreet, rehearsed duress signal can summon an appropriate response while prioritizing the employee's safety and avoiding overt escalation. Requiring physical resistance increases danger. A public announcement could provoke the aggressor, and retrospective reporting cannot provide immediate assistance during a coercion event.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Integrating threat modeling into an Agile development process
questions.performanceIndicator: Select an SDLC control that identifies design risk before implementation
questions.scenarioContext: A financial services development team delivers small application increments every two weeks. Security reviewers currently examine the completed application only before a major release, and recurring authorization design flaws are causing rework.
questions.prompt: What should the security manager recommend as the BEST way to address the recurring flaws while preserving the team's delivery model?

choices.A: Perform threat modeling during backlog refinement and update it when architecture or trust boundaries change.
choices.B: Require a full penetration test at the end of every two-week iteration before any code is merged.
choices.C: Move the existing security review to the user acceptance testing phase for every major release.
choices.D: Ask developers to document authorization defects after deployment so operations can monitor them.

questions.explanation: Integrating lightweight threat modeling into backlog refinement exposes authorization and trust-boundary weaknesses while design choices are still inexpensive to change. A penetration test every iteration is usually disproportionate and occurs after design and coding decisions. Moving the same review later does not prevent rework, and documenting deployed defects transfers rather than reduces risk.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Distinguishing product certification from authorization to operate
questions.performanceIndicator: Differentiate technical evaluation from management acceptance of residual risk
questions.scenarioContext: A government agency has completed a technical security evaluation of a new case-management system. The evaluation confirms that required controls are implemented, but several documented residual risks remain.
questions.prompt: Who should make the decision to permit the system to enter production?

choices.A: The lead developer who corrected the findings identified during testing.
choices.B: The assessor who performed the technical control evaluation.
choices.C: The designated authorizing official who can accept the residual risk.
choices.D: The quality assurance manager who confirmed that functional requirements were met.

questions.explanation: The authorizing official makes the risk-based decision to allow operation after considering the assessment results and residual risk. The assessor provides evidence but should not accept risk on management's behalf. Developers remediate defects, while quality assurance validates functionality; neither role ordinarily has the authority to approve operation based on enterprise risk.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Applying secure change management to emergency software fixes
questions.performanceIndicator: Balance urgent remediation with traceability, testing, and retrospective approval
questions.scenarioContext: A retail application contains a remotely exploitable flaw that is being actively targeted. The normal change approval board will not meet for four days, but the organization has a documented emergency change procedure.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST course of action?

choices.A: Deploy the fix immediately from a developer workstation and create the change record after the next board meeting.
choices.B: Wait for normal approval because bypassing the regular schedule creates an unacceptable audit exception.
choices.C: Disable all application logging temporarily to reduce load until the normal change can be approved.
choices.D: Use the emergency change process, document the risk and authorization, test the fix as feasible, preserve rollback capability, and obtain retrospective review.

questions.explanation: The emergency procedure provides controlled flexibility for an urgent security fix while retaining authorization, testing, traceability, rollback, and later review. An undocumented direct deployment breaks configuration control. Waiting leaves an actively exploited weakness exposed, and disabling logging neither corrects the flaw nor supports incident response.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Embedding security criteria in DevSecOps pipelines
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose risk-based automated gates that provide rapid developer feedback
questions.scenarioContext: A software firm is moving from monthly releases to continuous delivery. Executives want to prevent high-risk defects from reaching production without turning every deployment into a manual security review.
questions.prompt: Which control BEST supports this objective?

choices.A: Permit every build to deploy and rely on annual penetration testing to identify accumulated weaknesses.
choices.B: Define risk-based pipeline gates with automated security tests, protected overrides, and prompt feedback to developers.
choices.C: Require the chief information security officer to approve every source-code commit before integration.
choices.D: Perform security testing only in production because it most accurately represents the live environment.

questions.explanation: Risk-based automated gates align security checks with continuous delivery and can stop builds that exceed defined thresholds while preserving governed exceptions. Annual testing is too infrequent, executive approval of every commit is not scalable, and relying on production testing allows preventable defects to reach live systems.

questions.competency: VIII.A — Security in the Software Development Life Cycle
questions.skill: Planning security activities for application retirement
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify essential security controls during the disposal phase of the SDLC
questions.scenarioContext: A university is retiring a custom admissions application and migrating required records to a replacement service. The legacy system contains personal data, embedded service credentials, and archived source code.
questions.prompt: Which TWO actions are MOST important for secure retirement? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Preserve every legacy account indefinitely in case historical access is needed.
choices.B: Verify required records were migrated and retained according to legal and business requirements.
choices.C: Leave the legacy environment connected but remove its link from the public website.
choices.D: Sanitize residual data and revoke credentials, keys, accounts, and interfaces associated with the retired system.
choices.E: Delete all source code immediately, including materials subject to retention or contractual requirements.

questions.explanation: Secure retirement requires proof that records needed for business or legal purposes remain available and controlled, followed by sanitization and removal of access paths such as credentials, accounts, and interfaces. Indefinite accounts and continued connectivity preserve attack surface. Immediate indiscriminate deletion may violate retention, evidence, or contractual obligations.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Protecting source-code repositories against unauthorized changes
questions.performanceIndicator: Select layered repository controls that preserve integrity and accountability
questions.scenarioContext: An engineering organization discovers that a developer's compromised account was used to merge unreviewed code into a protected production branch. The repository recorded the account name, but no independent approval was required.
questions.prompt: Which improvement would MOST directly reduce the likelihood of the same event recurring?

choices.A: Require protected branches, independent pull-request approval, strong authentication, and restricted merge permissions.
choices.B: Increase the frequency of backups for the repository's underlying storage volume.
choices.C: Allow developers to share a release account so emergency merges are easier to coordinate.
choices.D: Export repository logs monthly and remove them from the active monitoring system.

questions.explanation: Protected branches, separation through independent review, strong authentication, and least-privilege merge rights directly address unauthorized code insertion through a compromised developer account. Backups improve recoverability but do not prevent an improper merge. Shared credentials weaken accountability, and delayed offline log review does not block the change.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Preventing injection through secure database access patterns
questions.performanceIndicator: Recognize the primary source-code control for separating data from commands
questions.scenarioContext: During code review, an analyst finds that a web application constructs database queries by concatenating values received from request parameters. Input validation exists in the browser, but the server accepts direct requests.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST corrective action?

choices.A: Add more client-side validation rules and obscure the database table names.
choices.B: Escape only the characters observed in the latest attack and retain string concatenation.
choices.C: Use parameterized queries on the server and apply server-side allow-list validation where appropriate.
choices.D: Encrypt the database files so injected statements cannot read stored information.

questions.explanation: Parameterized queries keep untrusted values separate from executable query structure, while server-side validation enforces expected input regardless of the client. Client-side checks can be bypassed, and attack-specific escaping is fragile. Storage encryption protects data at rest but does not prevent an authorized application connection from executing an injected query.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Managing secrets in continuous integration and delivery systems
questions.performanceIndicator: Select controls that prevent credential exposure in source and build artifacts
questions.scenarioContext: A media company learns that deployment credentials were committed to a private source repository and later copied into build logs. The repository is access-controlled, but many contractors can read it.
questions.prompt: Which response BEST addresses both the immediate exposure and the underlying development practice?

choices.A: Rename the credentials in the source file so automated scanners no longer recognize them.
choices.B: Remove the current line from the latest branch while retaining the same credentials for compatibility.
choices.C: Make the repository public so external researchers can report any additional exposed secrets.
choices.D: Revoke and rotate the exposed credentials, remove them from accessible history and logs, and retrieve future secrets from an approved secrets service at runtime.

questions.explanation: Because the credentials have been exposed, revocation and rotation are necessary; cleaning accessible history and logs limits continued disclosure, and managed runtime retrieval prevents recurrence. Renaming does not protect a secret. Removing only the latest line leaves copies and valid credentials elsewhere. Expanding repository access increases the risk.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Reducing memory-safety risk in native code
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize systemic controls for recurring unsafe memory operations
questions.scenarioContext: A manufacturer maintains a large native-code service that has suffered repeated out-of-bounds memory defects. Rewriting the entire service is not currently feasible, but new modules are still being added.
questions.prompt: Which strategy would provide the BEST sustainable risk reduction?

choices.A: Adopt memory-safe languages for suitable new modules, enable compiler and runtime protections, and prioritize review and testing of unsafe interfaces.
choices.B: Depend exclusively on developer training because automated controls cannot detect memory defects reliably.
choices.C: Disable crash reporting so attackers receive less information about exploitable conditions.
choices.D: Accept all existing memory defects until the organization can fund a complete rewrite.

questions.explanation: A layered migration strategy reduces new exposure through memory-safe implementations while hardening and scrutinizing the native-code boundary that must remain. Training is useful but insufficient as the sole control. Disabling crash reports impairs detection and diagnosis, and deferring all treatment leaves known systemic risk unaddressed.

questions.competency: VIII.B — Security Controls in Development Ecosystems and Secure Coding
questions.skill: Hardening software build environments against artifact tampering
questions.performanceIndicator: Choose controls that establish build provenance and artifact integrity
questions.scenarioContext: A technology cooperative cannot determine whether a released package was produced from the approved source commit because engineers build release artifacts on individually configured workstations.
questions.prompt: What should be implemented FIRST to establish trustworthy and repeatable releases?

choices.A: Allow each engineer to document local build settings in a personal procedure file.
choices.B: Use a controlled, isolated, reproducible build pipeline that records source provenance and signs verified artifacts.
choices.C: Compare the size of each release package with the previous version before distribution.
choices.D: Store unsigned release packages in a directory that only the development team can access.

questions.explanation: A controlled and reproducible pipeline ties an artifact to reviewed source and build inputs, while provenance records and signing support integrity verification after the build. Personal documentation cannot ensure identical or uncompromised environments. File size is not a reliable integrity check, and restricted storage without verification does not prove origin.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Selecting complementary application security testing techniques
questions.performanceIndicator: Match testing methods to source visibility and runtime behavior
questions.scenarioContext: A travel services company wants earlier detection of insecure code paths and also wants to observe authentication and session behavior while its web application is running in a test environment.
questions.prompt: Which TWO testing approaches BEST satisfy these distinct objectives? Select 2 of the 5 options below.

choices.A: Static application security testing of source or compiled code during development.
choices.B: Dynamic application security testing against the running test application.
choices.C: A financial audit of software licensing expenditures.
choices.D: A physical inspection of the test environment's network cabling.
choices.E: A business impact analysis of the travel reservation process.

questions.explanation: Static testing can identify insecure code paths early without executing the application, while dynamic testing evaluates the exposed behavior of the running application, including session and authentication handling. Licensing audits, cabling inspections, and business impact analysis may serve other objectives but do not meet the two stated software-testing needs.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Governing vulnerable open-source dependencies
questions.performanceIndicator: Apply risk-based software composition analysis and exception management
questions.scenarioContext: Software composition analysis identifies a severe vulnerability in an open-source parsing library used by several internal applications. A fixed version exists, but one critical application cannot immediately upgrade because of an incompatibility.
questions.prompt: What is the BEST response by the application security manager?

choices.A: Suppress the finding for all applications because one application cannot upgrade immediately.
choices.B: Upgrade compatible applications, assess exploitability and exposure for the exception, apply compensating controls, assign an owner and deadline, and monitor remediation.
choices.C: Remove the library inventory so future scans do not generate repeated findings.
choices.D: Replace all open-source components with internally written code before addressing the vulnerability.

questions.explanation: The best response reduces risk promptly where upgrades are feasible and governs the incompatible application through an evidence-based exception, compensating controls, ownership, and a remediation deadline. A broad suppression ignores differing exposure. Removing inventory destroys visibility, and replacing all open-source code is disproportionate and delays treatment of the known vulnerability.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Evaluating security evidence for acquired cloud software
questions.performanceIndicator: Prioritize risk-relevant supplier assurance over unsupported claims
questions.scenarioContext: A human resources department plans to acquire a cloud service that will process sensitive employee records. The provider offers a marketing security summary but will not share detailed controls, independent assessment evidence, incident obligations, or subcontractor information.
questions.prompt: What should the security professional recommend NEXT?

choices.A: Approve the service because a cloud provider is responsible for every security control.
choices.B: Run source-code analysis against the provider's public website and treat the result as complete assurance.
choices.C: Perform risk-based supplier due diligence and require appropriate evidence and contractual terms before approval.
choices.D: Accept the marketing summary if the business owner agrees to use a strong password.

questions.explanation: Sensitive employee data warrants due diligence proportionate to the risk, including credible assurance evidence, defined responsibilities, incident terms, data handling requirements, and relevant subcontractor transparency. Cloud use does not transfer all accountability. Testing a public interface cannot establish the provider's full control environment, and a strong password does not address supplier governance risks.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Securing application programming interface authorization
questions.performanceIndicator: Identify object-level authorization enforcement requirements
questions.scenarioContext: Testing shows that an authenticated customer can change an order identifier in an application programming interface request and retrieve another customer's order. The gateway correctly validates the user's access token.
questions.prompt: Which remediation MOST directly corrects the underlying weakness?

choices.A: Require the API to verify on every request that the authenticated principal is authorized for the specific requested object.
choices.B: Increase the access token length without changing the service's authorization logic.
choices.C: Encode order identifiers so customers cannot easily recognize their format.
choices.D: Add transport encryption between the gateway and the application service.

questions.explanation: Valid authentication does not prove authorization to a particular record. The service must enforce object-level authorization for each request using the authenticated identity and requested resource. Longer tokens and encoded identifiers do not repair the missing access decision, while transport encryption protects data in transit but does not prevent an authenticated user from requesting another user's object.

questions.competency: VIII.C — Assessing Software Security and Acquired Software Risk
questions.skill: Preserving accountability for software changes
questions.performanceIndicator: Design change logging that supports detection and investigation of unauthorized modifications
questions.scenarioContext: After unauthorized business logic appeared in a production application, investigators found that deployment logs could be edited by the same administrators who performed releases and contained no reliable link to approved change records.
questions.prompt: Which control enhancement would BEST improve future accountability?

choices.A: Let release administrators correct log entries after deployment so the record matches the final system state.
choices.B: Record only failed deployments because successful releases are already represented by the running code.
choices.C: Store deployment logs on each application server and overwrite them whenever storage becomes limited.
choices.D: Send tamper-evident deployment events to a separately controlled log system and correlate them with identities, artifacts, approvals, and timestamps.

questions.explanation: Separately controlled, tamper-evident logging reduces the ability of release administrators to alter evidence and creates an auditable chain connecting a person, approved change, deployed artifact, and time. Editable local logs lack independence, recording only failures omits critical activity, and routine overwriting undermines investigations and retention requirements.
